facts.statement: Barawertornis is an extinct genus of bird.
facts.quote: genus: Barawertornis

facts.statement: The only species in the genus Barawertornis is B. tedfordi.
facts.quote: species: tedfordi

facts.statement: Fragmentary remains of a dromornithid were first reported from the Carl Creek Limestone in Queensland in 1968 by Richard H. Tedford.
facts.quote: In 1968, the fragmentary remains of a dromornithid were reported from the Carl Creek Limestone of Riversleigh, Queensland by American palaeontologist Richard H. Tedford.

facts.statement: Patricia Vickers-Rich established the genus and species Barawertornis tedfordi in 1979 based on remains found by Richard H. Tedford.
facts.quote: Some of these remains, in addition to others, were used by Patricia Vickers-Rich in 1979 as the basis for a new genus and species, Barawertornis tedfordi.

facts.statement: Skull material was referred to Barawertornis in a 2016 study by Trevor Worthy and colleagues.
facts.quote: A study published in 2016 by Trevor Worthy and colleagues referred skull material to Barawertornis.

facts.statement: The genus name Barawertornis combines an Aboriginal word for 'ground' and the Ancient Greek word for 'bird'.
facts.quote: The genus name is a combination of an Aboriginal word for "ground" (Barawerti), although no particular language was specified, and the Ancient Greek ornis ("bird").

facts.statement: The species name tedfordi honors Richard H. Tedford for his discoveries of tertiary avian fauna in Australia.
facts.quote: The species name was chosen to honour Richard H. Tedford, for their discoveries of tertiary avian fauna in Australia.

facts.statement: Barawertornis lived during the Oligocene and Miocene epochs in Queensland and South Australia.
facts.quote: Barawertornis is an extinct genus of cassowary-sized dromornithid known from Oligocene and Miocene deposits in Queensland and South Australia.

facts.statement: Barawertornis shows anatomical adaptations for a running lifestyle.
facts.quote: It shows adaptations towards a cursorial lifestyle.

facts.statement: Barawertornis was likely a browser that ate leaves and fruit, similar to other dromornithids.
facts.quote: Like other dromornithids, Barawertornis was probably a folivorous and frugivorous browser.

facts.statement: A caudal intermuscular line is present on most Barawertornis femurs but absent in specimen QM F30352.
facts.quote: A caudal intermuscular line is present in most femurs referred to Barawertornis, but is absent in QM F30352.

facts.statement: The external femoral condyle of Barawertornis is about one-third the width of the internal condyle.
facts.quote: The external condyle is less wider than the internal condyle, being one-third of its width.

facts.statement: The shaft of the Barawertornis tibiotarsus is slightly curved from side to side.
facts.quote: The shaft of the tibiotarsus is slightly curved from side-to-side (mediolaterally).

facts.statement: A distal vascular foramen is present in Barawertornis tedfordi but absent in most Dromornis stirtoni specimens.
facts.quote: A distal vascular foramen is present in B. tedfordi, but absent in most specimens of Dromornis stirtoni.

facts.statement: The Barawertornis pterygoid has a dorsal process running above the quadrate articulation, a feature also seen in Dromornis planei.
facts.quote: The pterygoid has a dorsal process that runs above the quadrate articulation, which is a feature also seen in Dromornis planei.

facts.statement: The Barawertornis mandible lacks a caudal mandibular fenestra.
facts.quote: The mandible lacks the caudal mandibular fenestra.

facts.statement: The Barawertornis retroarticular process is deep and robust.
facts.quote: The retroarticular process is deep and robust.

facts.statement: Although unknown, the Barawertornis rostrum likely resembled that of Genyornis due to similarly slender and narrow mandibles.
facts.quote: Although the rostrum isn't known, it probably resembled that of Genyornis as its mandibles were similarly slender and dorsoventrally narrow.

facts.statement: Barawertornis tedfordi is the smallest known dromornithid species, weighing between 26.9 and 79 kg.
facts.quote: B. tedfordi is currently the smallest known species of dromornithid, comparable in size to the cassowaries and ranging in weight from 26.9 to 79 kg (59.3 to 174.1 lbs).

facts.statement: Barawertornis was originally assigned to the family Dromornithidae and placed in the subfamily Barawertornithinae.
facts.quote: In its description, Barawertornis was assigned to the family Dromornithidae and placed within its own subfamily Barawertornithinae.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Barawertornis belongs to the Ilbandornis lineage, with some researchers suggesting similarities in the crania support this.
facts.quote: Worthy et al. (2016) suggested that Barawertornis may have been part of the Ilbandornis lineage, due to the remarkable similarities of the crania.

facts.statement: A 2024 study suggests that Barawertornis, like other dromornithids, may have had adaptations for an aquatic feeding style.
facts.quote: A study published in 2024 by Phoebe McInerney and colleagues noted that Genyornis, and likely all dromornithids, showed adaptations to an aquatic feeding style.

facts.statement: Pathologies, including unhealed bite marks and fractures, were reported in Barawertornis fossils by Nguyen et al. in 2010.
facts.quote: Nguyen et al. (2010) reported pathologies in a femur and tarsometatarsus of Barawertornis.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that unhealed bite marks and fractures on a Barawertornis femur were caused by a crocodilian predator like Baru.
facts.quote: The femur shows unhealed bite marks and fractures, to which the authors hypothesised were likely caused by a predator such as the crocodilian Baru.

facts.statement: Gouges on a damaged Barawertornis tarsometatarsus are attributed to predators, scavengers, or trampling, though the exact cause is unknown.
facts.quote: A series of gouges are present on a heavily damaged tarsometatarsus. Although the exact cause is not known, it has been suggested that either predators, scavengers or animals trampling on the bone were what caused them.

facts.statement: Barawertornis fossils are found in Late Oligocene and Early Miocene limestone deposits at the Riversleigh World Heritage Area in Queensland.
facts.quote: Barawertornis is known from several Late Oligocene and Early Miocene limestone deposits at the Riversleigh World Heritage Area (WHA) in northwestern Queensland.

facts.statement: During the Late Oligocene, the Riversleigh habitat consisted of open forests with sclerophyllous vegetation and deciduous vine thickets.
facts.quote: At the time of the Late Oligocene, the area was covered in open forests. These forests would have featured sclerophyllous vegetation and deciduous vine thickets.

facts.statement: During the Early Miocene, the climate warmed and replaced open forests with gallery rainforest in the Barawertornis habitat.
facts.quote: As the climate warmed during the Early Miocene, open forests were then replaced by gallery rainforest.

facts.statement: Barawertornis tedfordi coexisted with the larger dromornithid Dromornis murrayi.
facts.quote: B. tedfordi coexisted alongside its larger relative, Dromornis murrayi.

facts.statement: Barawertornis fossils have been reported from the Leaf Locality of the Wipajiri Formation in northern South Australia.
facts.quote: Fossils attributable to this taxon have also been reported from the Leaf Locality of the Wipajiri Formation, northern South Australia.

facts.statement: The age of the Wipajiri Formation site is uncertain, with studies suggesting it dates to either the Early or Middle Miocene.
facts.quote: The precise age of the site is uncertain, with studies suggesting that it was either Early or Middle Miocene.

facts.statement: The environment of the Wipajiri Formation is unknown, with hypotheses ranging from temperate wet forest to a drier environment.
facts.quote: Little is also known about its environment, with researchers suggesting that it could have either been temperate wet forest or an, as yet, unknown, drier environment.

facts.statement: Barawertornis belongs to the extinct family Dromornithidae.
facts.quote: familia: †Dromornithidae

facts.statement: The genus Barawertornis was described by P. Rich in 1979.
facts.quote: genus_authority: P. Rich, 1979

facts.statement: Barawertornis tedfordi was an extinct flightless bird of the family Dromornithidae that lived from the Oligocene to the Miocene.
facts.quote: Barawertornis tedfordi es un género extinto de ave no voladora de la familia Dromornithidae, que vivió desde el Oligoceno al Mioceno.

facts.statement: Fossils of Barawertornis found in Riversleigh, Queensland, indicate it inhabited Australia.
facts.quote: Sus fósiles se han encontrado en Riversleigh, Queensland, lo cual indica que habitó en Australia.

facts.statement: Barawertornis was first described in 1979 by Patricia Vickers-Rich.
facts.quote: Fue descrito por primera vez en 1979 por Patricia Vickers-Rich.

facts.statement: Barawertornis was the smallest dromornithid, comparable in size to a cassowary, weighing between 80 and 95 kg.
facts.quote: Fue el dromornítido más pequeño, de tamaño comparable al de un casuario, llegando a pesar entre 80 y 95 kg.

facts.statement: Barawertornis was a runner, likely a herbivore, and inhabited Australian forests.
facts.quote: Era corredor, probablemente herbívoro y habitaba en los bosques de Australia.

facts.statement: Barawertornis lived between 23.04 and 15.98 million years ago (Aquitanian to Burdigalian stages).
facts.quote: Time range: Aquitanian to Burdigalian (23.04 to 15.98 million years ago)
